1476.text: In Ezra.10.1 and Neh.1.6, H3034 appears in Hithpael as 'confession' rather than the more common 'thanksgiving' sense -- a marked divergence from the base Hiphil gloss of praise/thanks. Here the impact is penitential: Ezra's confession is paired with weeping and prostration over the people's sin, and Nehemiah's confession covers Israel's national sin -- contrasting with the celebratory 'give thanks' occurrences (Ps.86.12, Ps.28.7) where the same root denotes joyful praise. This shows the lemma's bifurcated stem-based sense split.

1480.text: In Neh.1.6, confession (H3034) co-occurs with M41 (attentive/hear), M42 (prayer), M36 (servant), M56 (sin, twice). Confession functions as the specific content of the prayer being lifted, naming the sin for which attentive hearing is sought -- prayer is the vehicle, confession is the substantive act naming the wrong, and the servant-language frames the posture of the one confessing.

1828.text: In Neh.1.6 'confessing' likewise renders the penitential sense (confession of the sins of Israel), aligning with Ezra.10.1 rather than the thanksgiving/praise occurrences -- confirming a real bifurcation in usage across this cluster's own verse set between praise-occurrences and confession-occurrences of the same root.

1833.text: Adding to the prior finding for Neh.1.6: from confession's own vantage, it functions here as embedded WITHIN prayer (M42) rather than alongside it as a separate act -- confession is the specific content-clause of the prayer being offered, making it subordinate in form but central in substance to what is prayed.

1837.text: In Neh.1.6 Nehemiah (the speaking 'I', party) initiates the confessing operation, directed toward God (addressed as 'you'), naming the sins of the people of Israel including himself and his father's house.

3203.text: Within the confession-branch occurrences themselves, a further distinction is visible by stem/subject: Lev.16.21 (Qal-tq, Aaron confessing the people's sin OVER the scapegoat) and Num.5.7/Lev.26.40/Lev.5.5 (individual or corporate confession as a required legal/cultic act tied to restitution or covenant curse) represent a ritual-legal register, whereas Dan.9.20, Neh.1.6, Ezra.10.1, Neh.9.3, Dan.9.4 represent a personal/intercessory-prayer register (confession embedded within extended penitential prayer, weeping, and prostration) -- both are 'confession' but differ in whether the act is a discrete ritual requirement or an extended devotional/intercessory posture.

6776.text: In Ezek.33.6, H1875 ('require', of blood) co-occurs with M74 (watchman) and M56 (iniquity). First pass: darash here shifts from a seeking-verb to a judicial-demand sense -- it is God's requiring of accountability for the negligent watchman's failure, standing over against M74 (the watchman's duty) and M56 (the iniquity that occasions the death), naming the reckoning rather than the fault or the office.

6785.text: In Ezek.33.6, H1875 ('require') is tagged M83 only, not role-T3. The verse's own T3 operation words (blow, warned, comes, takes) are performed by/against the watchman (M74, a party role) and the people (T11 party) -- God's 'requiring' of blood stands as the covenantal consequence attached to, but grammatically outside, the T3-tagged action set.

7075.text: The 'require' surface form (Deut.18.19, Ezek.34.10, Mic.6.8, Ezek.20.40, Ezek.33.6, Deut.23.21, Gen.9.5) diverges sharply from the consultation sense: here H1875 denotes a superior party (God) formally demanding an accounting, exacting a debt, or requiring conduct/contributions from an inferior party -- the direction of the inquiry is inverted (God is the one requiring, not the one consulted), showing this single root spans both 'humans formally consulting a superior' AND 'a superior formally demanding of an inferior,' unified by the notion of a binding, authoritative claim being pressed rather than a casual search.

The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" 16491.text: 13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

19939.text: Turned toward it from far off: For those far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of prayer. The turning happens in the enemy's land. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is turned toward what God chose. Solomon prays it before the one who knows hearts: *"for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind"* (8:39). He also asks God to do the turning: *"that he may incline our hearts to him"* (8:58).; Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb. He asks God to remember his word to Moses: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Neh 1:9). Here the return is to God himself, and the place is where he brings those who return. Nehemiah's own part comes first: he *"sat down and wept and mourned for days"* (1:4), and confessed *"Even I and my father's house have sinned"* (1:6).

He also recalls David's heart: *"you did well that it was in your heart"* (v18). David was not allowed to build (v19).; The prayer that follows is a run of cases. In each, someone far from the house prays toward it, and Solomon asks God to hear in heaven. The heart is named throughout: *"each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house"* (v38); *"render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind)"* (v39); *"that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land"* (v40); The case of v48 is the hardest one, captivity: *"If they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy"* (v46). Then the inner turning, in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (v47). Literally, "bring it back to their heart" (*šûb*, H7725N, with the heart).; *"and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (v47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name"* (v48); "Repent" in v47 and v48 is *šûb* (*to return: repent*; H7725O), the same verb as "turn their heart". The turning happens in the enemy's land, far from the city. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is directed toward the chosen city.

20363.text: Job 7:15: "so that I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones": > Q1 citation: ❗ Needs attention. Ch 2 *Wanting to die* is accurate. The 10.7 working note (*Expected additions*) puts "Job's own words about choosing (Job 7:15 …)" under *Choices weighed by another*. No one weighs this choice: it is Job's own would-be choice, spoken to God in complaint. It belongs with the next bullet, *Choosing between death and life*. This is a working note, not narrative text.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: new. Corroborates Ch 2 *Wanting to die*. New: the soul (*nepheš*) is the chooser; the choice is set off by terror sent in dreams (v14); it is spoken to God, not acted on.; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M47 soul (H5315I): yes, for Ch 5 *The soul*: the soul as the one that would choose (#1979). M25 death: carried in Ch 2.; Job speaks *"in the anguish of my spirit … in the bitterness of my soul"* (v11). The choice follows from what is done to him at night: *"When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions, so that I would choose strangling and death"* (vv13–15). He goes on: *"I loathe my life; I would not live forever. Leave me alone"* (v16).; The ESV "I" in v15 is *nepheš* (H5315I): in the Hebrew it is the soul that would choose. It is a choice the soul would make. Job does not act on it.; It comes out of terror, and it is spoken to God: *"Why have you made me your mark?"* (v20).

20373.text: Philippians 1:22: "Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell": > Q1 citation: ✅ Accurate. Ch 7 *Flesh* quotes "If I am to live in the flesh …" for flesh as bodily life. Ch 2 quotes vv23–24 for Paul weighing life and death. Both accurate.; >; > Q2 M64: Include: new. New for 10.7: a choice between two goods that "I cannot tell"; his desire set against others' need; settled by being "convinced" and coming to "know" (v25), not by an act of choosing. Corroborates Ch 2.; >; > Q3 other M-codes: M25 live and M47 flesh: carried in Ch 2 and Ch 7. In the passage, v23 "My desire is to depart": yes, for 10.6 *Wanting* (desire weighed against others' need).; Paul writes from prison: *"to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain"* (v21). Then: *"If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell"* (v22); *"I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better"* (v23); *"But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (v24); *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (v25); The choice is held open between two goods. His own desire leans one way, and others' need leans the other. He is "hard pressed".; He does not settle it by choosing. He settles it by being "convinced" and coming to "know".

21278.text: Aloud here only carries a public announcement or summons; no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21296.text: Being silent is a person's, or God's, holding back of speech for a reason the verse shows: submission, fear, shame, awe, wisdom, obedience, waiting, or failure to speak up; or the refusal of it (anguish, praise, the watchmen's duty).

21314.text: Called is the standing given by God's call (the vocation); it is what diligence, worthiness or walking is directed at, not an inner operation in itself.

21356.text: Dealt is God's own act of dealing with a person or people according to what they are or have done, or according to his own faithfulness or love; it bears on them and is the outward act upon them.

21390.text: Old here dates a thing to the past (of old, the days of old, from of old) or names the people or prophets of old; no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21434.text: Wrath is here the anger, wrath or fury of God against persons or nations (kindled, poured out, turned away, executed, provoked); it is God's own act upon them, and bears on their inner response, which other words of the verse name, if at all.

21435.text: Wrath is here the anger, wrath, rage or fury of a person or people: a state of the heart aroused against another, a thing or God, named by the word itself.

21441.text: Consecrated here is the holiness or sacredness of a place, day, offering, oil, writing or thing set apart (a holy place, a sacred gift, the holy mountain); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.

21476.text: Righteousness is here righteousness given or reckoned to a person (counted as righteousness, the righteousness of God through faith, justification); it names the standing received, not an inner operation of its own.

21514.text: Choicest here describes the excellence of a thing, or persons or things selected as the best (choice silver, the choicest cedars, chosen warriors, 700 chosen men); no inner-being operation is voiced by it.
